grid.title: Spoons in hot water: {metal}
grid.unknown: how hot the top of the handle becomes

metal.label: a copper spoon
metal.note: Copper has the highest thermal conductivity of the common metals, so the handle becomes almost as hot as the water.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of the elements (copper 401 W/(m·K) at 300 K)
source.note: diffusivity k/(rho c) from the same handbook: 8960 kg/m3, 385 J/(kg·K)

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of the elements (aluminium 237 W/(m·K) at 300 K)
CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of alloys (cartridge brass 109 W/(m·K))
CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of alloys (AISI 304 stainless steel 16.2 W/(m·K))

metal.label: a glass rod in place of a spoon
metal.note: Glass is a poor conductor: the top of the rod stays at room temperature.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of common materials (soda-lime glass 1.05 W/(m·K))

metal.label: a wooden spoon
metal.note: This is why cooking spoons are made of wood.

source.title: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of common materials (oak across the grain 0.17 W/(m·K))
CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, thermal conductivity of common materials (nylon 6/6 0.25 W/(m·K))
